```{r setup}
library(pilotr)
```

Simulation-based power addresses how often an analysis would detect an effect if the world
matched the specification exactly. pilotr estimates this by repeatedly simulating from the
ground-truth specification, fitting the analysis model and recording the proportion of
significant results. Beyond power, it reports the design-analysis quantities of Gelman and
Carlin (2014), namely the Type S (sign) error and the Type M (magnitude, or exaggeration)
ratio.

> The mixed-effects examples below use small `n_sims`, and their results were precomputed with
> exactly the code shown and shipped with the package, so that the vignette builds quickly.
> `tools/vignette-caches.R` in the source repository regenerates them, and a test there fails if
> the seeds, the simulated data or the code shown change and the results are not regenerated. For
> real planning, we recommend `n_sims >= 200`, with more replicates for stable Type S and Type M
> estimates.

## Two-group Gaussian

The classic case has a closed-form analytic power, which the simulation matches.

```{r}
spec <- build_spec(list(
  name = "two_group", seed = 1, design_kind = "between", n_subject = 64,
  factor_name = "group", lev1 = "control", lev2 = "treatment",
  intercept = 100, effect = 5, family = "gaussian",
  resp_name = "score", sigma = 10))

pw <- power_design(spec, n_sims = 500)
unlist(pw[c("power", "type_s", "type_m", "true_effect", "mean_estimate")])
```

At roughly 50% power, the Type M ratio is well above 1. Conditional on significance, the
estimated effect is exaggerated, even though the average estimate over all replicates is
unbiased. This reflects the statistical-significance filter, which is precisely what design
analysis is meant to expose.

## Directional predictions

A preregistration that predicts the direction of an effect can test it one-sided. In
`power_design()`, `power_mixed()` and `power_curve_mixed()`, `alternative = "greater"` tests
whether the effect is positive and `alternative = "less"` whether it is negative. Here the
treatment group is predicted to score higher than the control group.

```{r}
pw_greater <- power_design(spec, n_sims = 500, alternative = "greater")
unlist(pw_greater[c("power", "type_s", "type_m")])
```

The one-sided p-value comes from the same t as the two-sided one, and it is half the two-sided
p-value when the estimate lies in the predicted direction. A one-sided test at α = 0.05
therefore rejects in exactly the replicates in which the two-sided test at 0.10 rejects with the
estimate in that direction. Its power of `r round(pw_greater$power, 3)` exceeds the two-sided
`r round(pw$power, 3)` above. Type S and Type M are taken over the replicates significant in
the predicted direction. Type S is therefore 0 by construction, and Type M,
`r round(pw_greater$type_m, 2)`, is the exaggeration among the replicates that would support the
prediction. Results from earlier versions of pilotr were two-sided. In the direction of the true
effect, a one-sided power at α is the two-sided power at 2α times one minus the Type S at 2α.

## Crossed mixed-effects designs

A feature that distinguishes pilotr from a marginal simulator is power estimation for crossed
by-subject and by-item designs. The R interface derives the analysis model from the
specification, fits it with `lme4`/`lmerTest` and tests each fixed effect with Satterthwaite
degrees of freedom.

```{r priming-spec}
spec_c <- build_spec(list(
  name = "priming", seed = 1, design_kind = "within", include_items = TRUE,
  n_subject = 24, n_item = 18,
  factor_name = "condition", lev1 = "related", lev2 = "unrelated",
  intercept = 6, effect = 0.06,
  subj_int_sd = 0.12, subj_slope_sd = 0.04, subj_corr = 0.2,
  item_int_sd = 0.08, item_slope_sd = 0.02, item_corr = -0.1,
  family = "shifted_lognormal", resp_name = "RT", sigma = 0.3, shift = 200))
```

The priming design above is fully crossed, so each of the 24 participants sees all 18 items in
both conditions, 864 trials in all. A counterbalanced study, in which each participant sees
each item in one condition only, has half the observations and lower power. Plan such a study
by adding `counterbalance = TRUE` to the `build_spec()` call above. The factor `condition` then
sets `counterbalance`, a field of specification version 0.4 that rotates the conditions over
participants and items as a Latin square does (see
[counterbalanced lists](https://github.com/pablobernabeu/pilotr/blob/main/spec/SPEC.md#counterbalanced-lists)).
The two-list encoding among the
[worked encodings](https://github.com/pablobernabeu/pilotr/blob/main/spec/SPEC.md#worked-encodings)
of the specification writes the same design for releases that read no version above 0.3.

The model fitted to each replicate is the one the specification implies, here the maximal model
for the design, with by-subject and by-item intercepts and slopes for the condition.

```{r}
model_formula(spec_c)
```

`effect` is the contrast column that `model_data()` adds for the condition, coded −0.5 for
related and 0.5 for unrelated, so its coefficient is the unrelated condition minus the related
one. `.y` is the response on the scale of the specification's coefficients, which for this
shifted lognormal response is log(RT − `r spec_c$response$shift`), the logarithm of the reaction
time less its shift.

```{r power-mixed, eval = FALSE}
# A tiny replicate count keeps the vignette fast. Use 200 or more for real planning.
pm <- power_mixed(spec_c, n_sims = 20)
pm
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
# The result of running exactly the chunk above, precomputed by tools/vignette-caches.R and
# shipped with the package so that the vignette builds within CRAN's check-time budget.
pm <- readRDS("power-mixed-cache.rds")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
pm
```

`power` is the proportion of significant results among the replicates that returned an
estimate, which the result counts as `n_returned`, here `r pm$n_returned` of `r pm$n_sims`. The
remaining counts describe the fits without entering `power`. `n_converged` counts the fits that
returned an estimate with neither a warning nor a singular fit, `r pm$n_converged` here, and
`n_singular` those whose variance estimates sat on a boundary, `r pm$n_singular` here. Singular
and warning fits are kept in `power`, since their fixed-effect estimates remain interpretable
and discarding them would bias the result. A large `n_singular` says that the model is richer
than the design can support at this sample size, which is common in small crossed designs and
worth reporting beside the power.

`power_mixed()` carries its own simulation loop over the portable specification, with no other
power package underneath it. It covers territory pioneered by
[simr](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.12504) (Green and MacLeod, 2016) and
[mixedpower](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-021-01546-0) (Kumle, Vo and Draschkow, 2021). pilotr
differs in being driven by the cross-language specification, in reporting Type S and Type M
errors alongside power and in built-in parallelisation.

## A preregistered simplification rule

The power above is that of an analysis that reports the maximal model whatever its fit. Many
analysis plans preregister a rule instead: fit the maximal model, and when the fit is singular,
drop the correlations between the random effects, then the slopes
([Barr et al., 2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2012.11.001);
[Matuschek et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2017.01.001)). Each replicate is then
analysed with a model that depends on its data, so the rule has a power and a Type I error rate
of its own. `model_formula()` builds the two simpler models, `"zcp"`, the zero-correlation model,
and `"intercepts"`, with random intercepts alone.

```{r}
model_formula(spec_c, "zcp")
model_formula(spec_c, "intercepts")
```

Given the names of the three models as `formula`, `power_mixed()` and `precision_design()` fit
them to each replicate in turn, as the rungs of a ladder. Each replicate keeps the first fit that
is not singular, or the intercepts-only fit when every rung is singular, and
`fallback = "warning"` also moves on from a fit with a convergence warning. The result gives the
share of the replicates analysed at each rung, and its fit counts describe the fits that were
kept.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pm_rule <- power_mixed(spec_c, formula = c("maximal", "zcp", "intercepts"),
                       fallback = "singular", n_sims = 200)
pm_rule$rung_shares
```

A rule that can end on random intercepts alone ignores, whenever it gets there, how much the
effect varies over subjects and items, and a test that ignores that variation rejects a true null
hypothesis too often (Barr et al., 2013). Run the null condition through the same ladder to see
how often. `design_conditions()` puts it first.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sweep_spec(spec_c, "fixed$coefficients", design_conditions(effect = 0.06),
           power_mixed, formula = c("maximal", "zcp", "intercepts"), n_sims = 200)
```

`tools/calibration/simplification_rule.R` in the source repository runs these replicates, 200 in
each condition, and analyses each of them with the maximal model, with the rule and with random
intercepts alone. With the effect, the maximal model was singular in 152 of the 200 replicates.
The rule kept the maximal fit in the other 48, and of the 152 it kept the zero-correlation fit in
23 and the intercepts-only fit in 129. It raised power from 0.69 to 0.735, each with a Monte
Carlo standard error of about 0.03. Random intercepts alone gave 0.835, but not all of that gain
is real. Relative to the spread of its estimates, the intercepts-only model reported standard
errors about 15% smaller than the maximal model did, in both conditions. In the null condition,
the three analyses rejected in 2, 3 and 6 of the 200 replicates, where a test at its nominal
level would reject in 10. The slopes of this design are small beside its residual variation,
which leaves the intercepts-only model little to ignore. Where the effect varies more over
subjects or items, it ignores more, and the null condition shows what that costs.

## Which model each family gets

`power_mixed()` and `precision_design()` choose the fitter by the response family, so that the
estimates are on the scale the specification's coefficients are written on. The mean estimate,
Type M and the region of practical equivalence then compare like with like. A model without
random effects, such as that of a between-subjects design with one row per subject, is fitted by
`lm()` or `glm()`. Each result names its fitter and test in `fitter`.

| Family | R `power_mixed()` | R `precision_design()` | Python `power_mixed` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gaussian`, `exgaussian` | `lmerTest::lmer()`, Satterthwaite *t* | `lme4::lmer()`, Wald interval | MixedLM, Wald *z* |
| `lognormal`, `shifted_lognormal` | as above, on the log scale | as above, on the log scale | MixedLM on the log scale, Wald *z* |
| `bernoulli` | `lme4::glmer()`, binomial, Wald *z* | `lme4::glmer()`, Wald interval on the logit scale | linear model on the response scale, a warning, no mean estimate or Type M, and no Type S for an interaction |
| `poisson` | `lme4::glmer()`, Poisson, Wald *z* | `lme4::glmer()`, Wald interval on the log scale | as for `bernoulli` |
| `ordinal`, `beta` | linear model on the response scale, a warning, no mean estimate or Type M, and no Type S for an interaction | linear model on the response scale, a warning, no ROPE decisions (the interval width stays) | as for `bernoulli` |

A Wald *z* treats the variance components as known. It is the test
[Bolker et al. (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tree.2008.10.008) recommend for the fixed
effects of a GLMM without overdispersion. With few subjects or items, however, it rejects more
often than its nominal level ([Li and Redden, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-015-0026-x)),
so the power of a small accuracy or count design is somewhat overstated.

Ordinal and Beta outcomes have no frequentist model here yet, so their power is that of the
linear model's test and their Type S compares signs alone. A bounded response compresses
differences near the ends of its range, so an interaction can change sign between the two
scales, and its Type S is withheld. `generate_design_analysis()` writes a Bayesian design
analysis for them, on the logit scale of their coefficients. Python's `power_mixed` fits the model
the specification implies, from ports of `model_formula()` and `model_data()`, with every random
effect as an independent variance component, so it leaves out the correlations that `lme4`
estimates here. It refuses a design without random effects, as its own guide describes.

## A power curve

The following sweep over the number of subjects reports power at each size.

```{r power-curve, eval = FALSE}
curve <- power_curve_mixed(
  spec_c,
  subject_ns = c(8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 44, 56),
  n_sims = 50)
print(curve[, c("n_subject", "power", "power_lo", "power_hi", "type_m",
                "n_returned", "n_converged", "n_singular")], digits = 3)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
# The result of running exactly the chunk above, precomputed by tools/vignette-caches.R and
# shipped with the package so that the vignette builds within CRAN's check-time budget.
curve <- read.csv("power-curve-cache.csv")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
print(curve[, c("n_subject", "power", "power_lo", "power_hi", "type_m",
                "n_returned", "n_converged", "n_singular")], digits = 3)
```

The curve has a row for each sample size, with the power, Type S, Type M and fit counts that
`power_mixed()` reports, and the table shows some of its columns. `power_lo` and `power_hi` bound
the 95% Wilson interval of each power estimate, and the fit counts read as they do above, with
`n_returned` the denominator of power.

Each sample size draws its own replicates. Point *j* of a sweep over *J* sizes takes
`replicate_seeds(seed, J)[j]` as its seed, so no two points share their random numbers, as
`target_n()` assumes below when it fits them. Up to pilotr 0.3.1 every point took the
specification's own seed, which `seeds = "shared"` still does.

## The sample size the curve implies

The curve is a means to an end. What the analysis is run for is the sample size at which
power reaches the target, and that is the number a preregistration quotes. Reading it off the
table or the plot judges points whose Monte Carlo intervals overlap, and yields a bare figure
with no interval attached to it. `target_n()` fits the curve and inverts the fit, so the
crossing is estimated, and arrives with the uncertainty a simulated curve carries.

```{r}
solved <- target_n(curve, target = 0.8)
unlist(solved[c("n", "n_lo", "n_hi")])
```

Fifty replicates per point is few, and the interval says so. The fit is a binomial regression
of power on the square root of the sample size, weighted by the replicates behind each point,
and the interval is the delta-method interval that `MASS::dose.p()` computes for a fitted
`glm`. Nothing is extrapolated: a curve that never reaches the target within the sizes swept is
refused, and the refusal reports the range the sweep did cover.

For a curve swept over something other than sample size, `solve_curve()` is the general form,
with `transform = "identity"` where the axis is an effect size.

Plotting the curve and the solved size together shows what the solve has done.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.6, dev.args = list(bg = "transparent")}
# The transparent device canvas is what lets the page colour through. A ggplot
# theme alone cannot do it, since the device paints white underneath. The
# website's dark mode then inverts the figure's ink, so the axes and labels
# follow the theme and the figure carries no opaque matte.
library(ggplot2)
# Each power estimate is a proportion over the replicates that returned an
# estimate, and the curve carries its 95% Wilson interval, which the shaded
# band draws.
ggplot(curve, aes(n_subject, power)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  # The solved sample size and its interval. The dashed horizontal line marks
  # the target and the band marks where the curve reaches it.
  annotate("rect", xmin = solved$lo, xmax = solved$hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey60", alpha = .15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = solved$value, linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = power_lo, ymax = power_hi),
              alpha = .15, fill = "#2C6FB0") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2C6FB0", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2C6FB0", size = 2.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(N) ~ "subjects"), y = "Power") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  # theme_minimal still paints a white plot.background over the transparent
  # canvas, so both surfaces have to be cleared for the page colour to reach the
  # figure. The ink is left at its default, because the website inverts the
  # figure in dark mode, which turns the dark axis text light, whereas a fixed
  # mid-grey would be inverted into a muddy tan.
  theme(plot.background  = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
        panel.grid       = element_line(colour = "grey80"))
```

The shaded horizontal band along the curve is the Monte Carlo interval, the 95% Wilson interval
of each power estimate over its `n_returned` replicates. Unlike a band of 1.96 standard errors
either side, it stays between 0 and 1 and keeps a width where power reaches either. The vertical
band is the solved sample size and its own interval, which is what the dashed target line
invites the reader to guess at.

The solved size counts the participants whose data are analysed. Simulated data are complete,
with no attrition or exclusions. A study that expects to lose a proportion *p* of its
participants therefore recruits *N* / (1 − *p*), which is 67 for 60 analysed at 10% attrition.
Losses unrelated to the outcome cost power without biasing the estimates, and recruiting the
extra participants largely restores that power. Missingness that depends on the outcomes that
would have been observed, which pilotr does not simulate, can bias the estimates as well
([Rubin, 1976](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/63.3.581)).

## A sample-size justification

A preregistration, a registered report or a grant application has to justify the sample size it
asks for, and the solved size is only part of that justification.
[Lakens (2022, Table 4)](https://doi.org/10.1525/collabra.33267) also asks for the primary
analysis with its alpha and sidedness, the desired power, each effect size with the reason it was
chosen, and the power when the null hypothesis is true. A simulation adds items of its own: the
number of replicates, the fits that were singular or carried a warning and the Monte Carlo error
of every rate ([Morris, White and Crowther, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086)).
`power_report()` writes all of them in Markdown from a power result, the `target_n()` result and
the specification file, whose seed and checksum it records. The justification below is
illustrative.

```{r}
spec_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "priming.json")
writeLines(spec_json(spec_c), spec_file)
power_report(pm, solved = solved, spec_file = spec_file,
             justification = c(effect = paste(
               "A difference of 0.06 on the log scale, about 6% of the reaction time less",
               "its shift, the smallest effect of theoretical interest.")))
```

The rates in the report are those of `pm`, the 20 replicates at 24 subjects above, which keep the
vignette quick. A justification to submit pairs the solved size with a run at that size and with
enough replicates for planning. It adds the same analysis with the effect set to zero as
`null_result`, whose rejection rate shows whether the test holds its level in this design.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
at_n <- spec_c
at_n$units$subject$n <- solved$n
writeLines(spec_json(at_n), "priming.json")
null_n <- at_n
null_n$fixed$coefficients$effect <- 0
report <- power_report(power_mixed(at_n, n_sims = 500), solved = solved,
                       spec_file = "priming.json",
                       justification = c(effect = "Why an effect of this size matters."),
                       null_result = power_mixed(null_n, n_sims = 500))
cat(report, file = "justification.md")
```

Each rate's Monte Carlo standard error and Wilson interval are computed in the report from its
counts, and the Python twin's `power_report()` writes the same text from the same counts.

## Subjects and items

```{r, include = FALSE}
# The quantities the paragraphs below quote, read from the specification. recipe_subjects holds
# the subject counts that the recipe at the end of this section sweeps.
n_item <- spec_c$units$item$n
item_slope_sd <- spec_c$random$item$slopes$effect
subj_slope_sd <- spec_c$random$subject$slopes$effect
true_effect <- spec_c$fixed$coefficients$effect
se_floor <- item_slope_sd / sqrt(n_item)
recipe_subjects <- c(24, 36, 48)
subj_floor <- subj_slope_sd / sqrt(min(recipe_subjects))
```

The curve above adds subjects and keeps `r n_item` items, and in a crossed design the number of
items limits what more subjects can buy. When the effect of the condition varies from item to
item, as the by-item slope in the specification says it does, part of the standard error of the
effect comes from the items sampled. That part shrinks only as items are added. As subjects are
added, the standard error therefore falls towards a floor set by the number of items. Power
at a fixed number of items levels off below 1
([Westfall, Kenny and Judd, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000014);
[Judd, Westfall and Kenny, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-122414-033702)). In the
priming design, the floor is the by-item slope standard deviation over the square root of the
number of items, `r item_slope_sd` / √`r n_item` ≈ `r signif(se_floor, 2)`. The effect of
`r true_effect` is some `r round(true_effect / se_floor)` times that, so the ceiling lies far
above any target.

Where the ceiling is lower, a curve over subjects flattens towards it, and the probit curve that
`target_n()` fits rises towards 1 and cannot bend into the plateau. A curve that levels off near
the target can then be solved far from the true crossing. One that levels off just below the
target never crosses it, but Monte Carlo noise can lift a simulated power over the target, and
the curve can then be solved as though it crossed.

To compare designs that trade subjects for items, sweep the number of items at a few subject
counts and solve each of those curves for the number of items. Power over items levels off in the
same way. As items are added, the standard error falls towards the by-subject slope standard
deviation over the square root of the number of subjects, which at the smallest subject count
below is `r subj_slope_sd` / √`r min(recipe_subjects)` ≈ `r signif(subj_floor, 2)`. The effect is
some `r round(true_effect / subj_floor)` times that, so these curves too can rise well past the
target.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Not run here, since it fits 3,000 models: three subject counts, five item counts and
# 200 replicates at each. Each solve gives the number of items that reaches a power of
# 0.8 with that many subjects.
pairs <- lapply(c(24, 36, 48), function(n_subject) {
  spec <- spec_c
  spec$units$subject$n <- n_subject
  items <- sweep_spec(spec, "units$item$n", c(8, 12, 18, 27, 40), power_mixed,
                      n_sims = 200, .name = "n_item")
  solved <- target_n(items, target = 0.8)
  data.frame(n_subject = n_subject, n_item = solved$n,
             n_item_lo = solved$n_lo, n_item_hi = solved$n_hi)
})
do.call(rbind, pairs)
```

The pairs trace how many items each number of subjects needs, and the cheapest of them, given
what a subject and an item each cost, is the design to plan for.

## Parallel execution

Every power and precision analysis in pilotr takes a `workers` argument that spreads the
Monte Carlo replicates across local cores. Each replicate takes its own seed from
`replicate_seeds()`, so the results are identical to a serial run whatever the worker
count, and parallelisation costs nothing in reproducibility. The mixed-model fits dominate
the running time, which makes the speed-up close to linear in the number of cores. In a
sweep the worker pool is created once and reused across all sample sizes. The analyses also
take a cluster made with `parallel::makeCluster()` as `cl`, which `sweep_spec()` passes to
every point of an effect-size sweep in the same way.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
power_curve_mixed(
  spec_c, subject_ns = seq(20, 60, 10), n_sims = 500, workers = 8)
```

This design answers a serial bottleneck familiar from `simr::powerCurve()`, which this
package's maintainer previously worked around by splitting the sample-size grid across
separate jobs by hand and recombining the results afterwards
([Bernabeu, 2021](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/2021/parallelizing-simr-powercurve/)).
In pilotr the same gain takes one argument.

## A bridge to the Bayesian workflow

For a confirmatory Bayesian fit, `brms_bridge()` returns a ready-to-run `brms` model. It
provides the family, the fixed and random-effects formula, and a weakly-informative prior set,
all derived from the same specification, so that the planning model and the confirmatory model
remain consistent. The formula reads the contrast columns that `model_data()` adds, so the model
runs on `model_data(spec_c, simulate_design(spec_c))` or on collected data passed through
`model_data()`. Its priors are scaled to the response and to each of those columns, here on the
log scale on which the coefficients of a shifted lognormal act. Printing the result shows the model
as code to copy into a script; assigning it instead gives the same parts as `formula`, `family`
and `priors`, silently, for a caller assembling its own.

```{r}
brms_bridge(spec_c)
```

## See also

The [precision / ROPE vignette](precision-rope.html) covers design analysis against a region of
practical equivalence, where the question is whether an effect is large enough to matter.
